item.text: {"text":"Research supports fixed-length replacement diagnostics, but warns that unrealistic perturbations can distort importance estimates. [Learning Causal Explanations for Recommendation](https://csr21.github.io/xu-csr2021.pdf) replaces items while preserving history length; [CETD](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/20/11176) emphasizes temporal dependencies and proximity to observed histories. [Hase et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00786) show that replacement choices can introduce out-of-distribution effects. These findings support interpreting frozen-model perturbations as model sensitivity, without assuming they identify causal effects on user preferences.\n\nA proposed controlled design: within each user, replace equal-sized recent and older windows at their original positions using exactly the same replacement items and ordering; preserve padding, timestamps, candidates and readout. Common replacements balance inserted-item popularity, but removed-item popularity and contextual compatibility can still differ. Match original windows on training-frequency distributions and replacement-to-original popularity changes; restrict replacements to common support where both interventions have comparable title/description similarity and training-history transition likelihood, including window boundaries. Use training-only statistics and report matching tolerances, retained-user coverage and residual imbalance. Repeat paired draws across popularity strata and coherence thresholds; include unchanged-history controls and deliberately incoherent replacements as stress tests. Measure paired differences in target-score changes and rank displacement, with user-level bootstrap intervals and category-level results. This design is a synthesis of the literature: a persistent recent-versus-older gap under balanced, plausible replacements strengthens evidence for positional sensitivity, while gaps concentrated in low-likelihood perturbations suggest corruption sensitivity. Strict common-support filtering also narrows which histories the conclusion covers."}
